summary_md: Osnabrugge, Hobolt and Rodon (APSR 2021) ask whether legislators use emotive language strategically, raising it when a debate reaches voters rather than only colleagues. They score 958,925 UK House of Commons speeches (2001-2019) and 945,734 Irish Dail speeches (2002-2013) with a dictionary built from ANEW seed words (emotive = clearly positive or negative, neutral = neither) expanded through corpus-trained skip-gram embeddings; each speech gets percent emotive minus percent neutral words (mean 0.88, SD 8.95 on a -100 to 100 scale). OLS with MP-clustered errors shows Prime Minister's Questions speeches score 2.23 points higher than ordinary debates, and 1.56 to 1.66 higher within the same MP once MP fixed effects are added; the Queen's Speech opening day is similar, Ministerial Question Time is slightly lower, and topic fixed effects do not remove the gap. Ireland's Leaders' Questions shows 2.5 to 4.6. The electoral-cycle effect is tiny (0.015 per 100 days). The authors state the design is observational and cannot causally identify audience exposure. For Paul's systems the paper matters in two places. First, it is direct evidence that the same speaker's affect-word rates move with venue and audience, which bears on the lexical Big Five and affective-N slots: Melange pools social posts, floor speech and interviews per member before z-scoring, and the interview-to-floor N transfer already failed. It supports Paul's ask for venue-specific frameworks. Second, its valence-agnostic emotive score is closer to the unused lsd_charge option than to the live abs(net)/words intensity in the press pipeline, and its audience logic cautions that press-release heat may index performance for the public rather than commitment.

bearings.paper_claim: Within the same MP (MP fixed effects), PMQs speeches score 1.562 to 1.663 points higher on emotive-minus-neutral than other debates (Table 3 Models 3-5; speech-level SD 8.95), and the Queen's Speech opening day 2.064 in Model 5; venue, not speaker, shifts emotive word rates.
bearings.paper_location: Table 3, pp. 8-9; Figure 3, p. 9; descriptive stats p. 7
bearings.system_side: Default corpus pools social posts plus CREC floor speech plus INTERVIEW turns into one text list per member, then computes per-1000-word posemo, negemo, anx, anger and exclam rates and z-scores them within the corpus; genre is only a validation hook (BIG5_SOURCES), not a covariate. Members with different venue mixes therefore differ in affect rates partly for venue reasons.
bearings.code_ref: fec/members/big5_traits.py:36-73 (BIG5_SOURCES hook; default speech sources CREC and INTERVIEW plus social, pooled into texts[m]); fec/members/big5_traits.py:180-183 (posemo/negemo weights in E, ES, A, C)
bearings.transfer_conditions: Holds if US floor speech, interviews and social posts differ in audience exposure the way PMQs differs from ordinary Commons debate; the paper covers UK and Irish lower houses only, with a valence-agnostic emotive score rather than LIWC posemo/negemo. The speech-level shift is small (about 0.18 SD), but member-level venue mix can vary far more. Observational, not causal.

bearings.paper_claim: Emotive rhetoric is strategic and audience-dependent: the same legislators raise it in high-profile, voter-facing debates (UK PMQs +1.6 within MP; Ireland Leaders' Questions +2.5 to +4.6), so affect words in speech partly reflect venue strategy rather than a stable disposition.
bearings.paper_location: Theory pp. 3-4; Table 3 p. 8; Table 5 p. 12
bearings.system_side: affective_n is built only from INTERVIEW turns (LIWC i + negemo - posemo as convergent anchor plus LLM facets), and the recorded genre transfer of interview N to floor and hearing text failed (rho .050, .161). The paper supplies a plausible mechanism for that failure and supports keeping the slot interview-bound.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Explains, does not prove, the transfer failure: the paper tests average venue shifts, not whether member rank order of affect is preserved across venues, which is what rho measures. Does not license re-scoring floor text.

bearings.paper_claim: Emotiveness is measured valence-agnostically as percent emotive (clearly positive or negative ANEW words, 851 seeds) minus percent neutral (970 seeds), with the dictionary expanded by skip-gram embeddings trained on the corpus to 2,015 emotive and 2,095 neutral UK words, following Rice and Zorn.
bearings.system_side: The live press intensity is abs(lsd_net_norm) = abs(pos - neg)/words, so a release heavy in both positive and negative language nets toward zero. stage5_lsd.R already emits lsd_charge = (pos + neg)/words, a valence-agnostic intensity closer to the paper's construct, selectable when INTENSITY == charge but not the default. LSD2015 is a generic news dictionary with no domain expansion.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Applies if 'how heated' should mean emotional charge regardless of direction; the paper validates on parliamentary speech, not press releases, and its human-validation checks sit in appendices not in the extracted text. Switching intensity would change press_value and the Press pillar, a change-control decision for Paul, not a recommendation here.

bearings.paper_claim: Politicians are most emotive when addressing voters; emotive rhetoric trades off against credibility and is used as a persuasion tool aimed at the public audience (Hypothesis H, p. 4; supported in two parliaments).
bearings.system_side: press_value = stance sign x LSD intensity, so a member's signed press weight rises with how heated their own-domain releases are. Press releases are a uniformly public-facing venue, so per the paper the intensity term may index audience performance and messaging style more than strength of CU commitment.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Holds to the extent between-member intensity differences reflect style rather than commitment; the paper shows within-speaker venue shifts, not between-member style differences in one venue. Bears on the open question whether sign x intensity predicts behaviour better than sign alone.

gaps_exposed: No venue or genre adjustment in the lexical Big Five: affect-category rates are pooled across social, floor and interview text per member; a per-genre z-score or genre-mix covariate is absent (BIG5_SOURCES is a validation hook only).

Press intensity uses abs(net)/words, which cancels mixed-valence heat; the valence-agnostic lsd_charge option exists but has not been validated against human-coded intensity (open question on melange-stance.lsd-tone).
No test of whether stance sign x intensity predicts CU-aligned behaviour better than stance sign alone; the paper's audience logic makes that test more pressing.
No domain-expanded dictionary for congressional press or floor text; a Rice and Zorn style embedding expansion is on disk as a paper but unused.
flags: Observational design: the authors say they cannot causally identify the audience effect (p. 10); quote any use as association.

Pooled baseline (PMQs 2.226) mixes speakers and parties; quote the within-MP estimates (1.562 to 1.663, Table 3 Models 3-5) when citing a venue shift, with window UK 2001-2019 and denominator 958,925 speeches.
Abstract says about two million speeches; analysed samples are 958,925 UK (2001-2019) and 945,734 Irish (2002-2013) speeches; cite the body figures.
Appendices A-J (LIWC, positive/negative split, alternative scalings) are not in the extracted text and were not checked.
paul_alignment: Paul has no annotation on this work. The evidence agrees with his stated position on the lexical Big Five that Ramey-style scoring needs venue-specific frameworks: this paper shows the same legislators shift emotive word use by venue and audience. His note is not stale: the system still pools venues by default (big5_traits.py:36-73) with genre restriction only as a validation hook, while the affective-N slot stays interview-only after its transfer test failed, which is consistent with this paper.

related.why: Source of the 2001-2014 UK Hansard speech corpus and an earlier embedding-based emotion measure for the same parliament.
The paper's dictionary expansion follows Rice and Zorn's corpus-based embedding approach to specialised vocabularies.
Ramey infers stable traits from floor speech; this paper shows floor affect words shift with venue and audience, a confound for trait readings of the same text.
Measures emotional intensity of congressional speech from vocal pitch rather than words, an independent channel for a similar construct.
Studies emotional expression in US Congress speech and links it to legislative effectiveness, carrying the emotive-rhetoric construct into the US setting.
Alternative dictionary-plus-crowdcoding route to measuring negativity in political text, offering human validation this paper leaves to appendices.
Meta-analysis of LIWC to Big Five links; together they bound how much of a LIWC emotion rate is trait versus context.
